en: A Direct Commentary on the *Ālambanaparīkṣā* (Treatise Examining the Object of Cognition) Composed by the Bodhisattva Dignāga Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang
The practitioner Ouyi Zhixu explains that the single character "contemplation" (guan) refers to the wisdom capable of contemplating;
that is, the sixth consciousness together with the various wholesome mental factors such as correct understanding (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*).
By relying on the correct teachings and correct principles as the definitive standard, it ensures that regarding the object of contemplation, one does not fall into error or confusion.

The three characters "ālambana-pratyaya" (object-condition) refer to the objects of observation; that is, the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the mind-king (*citta*) and its mental factors (*caitta*).
Generally, all mind-kings and mental factors arise by depending upon four conditions: first, the direct causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), which is the seed (*bīja*);

second, the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), which is the preceding moment of active manifestation (*pravṛtti*); and third, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), which refers to the respective objects of consciousness.

The objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) transformed by oneself constitutes the fourth, the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), which includes the six sense organs as well as all other mental states and their concomitants (*citta-caitta*).

Now, among these four conditions, we discuss exclusively the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Furthermore, within all object-conditions, we speak specifically regarding the first five consciousnesses.
This is because the objects of the five sensory domains, which are perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), are the common concern of both ordinary people and non-Buddhists.

The followers of the Hīnayāna are deluded and lack understanding; they falsely reckon that there are real dharmas external to the mind. Consequently, they give rise to notions of grasping and rejecting, and they produce greed, hatred, and delusion.

Now, by means of correct reasoning through inference and comparison, it is evident that since [the object] is neither an atom nor a composite, there is not a single dharma external to the mind that can serve as an objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Thus, the objective condition is solely...
One clearly perceives that these are merely manifestations transformed by one's own consciousness.

Since they are solely the objective aspects (nimitta-bhāga) manifested by one's own consciousness, how could one allow thoughts of acceptance or rejection to arise, or give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion? This is the divine sword that shatters the dual attachments to self and phenomena.

It is the sharp axe that severs the delusions of affliction. The meaning of the word "treatise" (śāstra) can be understood as usual. Within the treatise, it first describes the two attachments to the combination of atoms;
this is the section on the "semblance of a valid proof. Following this, from the passage beginning with "Next, it clarifies that both are irrational," it proceeds to explain the refutation.
"This is the Gate of True Refutation. The subsequent explanation that "internal form is like external manifestation" and so forth establishes the correct meaning; this is the "Gate of True Proof.

All of these were composed by the Bodhisattva Dignāga, who, having realized true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) through fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), was able to establish true inference (*anumāna*) through subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) to enlighten later generations; thus it is called a *śāstra*. We...
Those who study this treatise should take this authentic teaching as their standard of authority.

During the two periods of six hours each day, they should constantly observe the five sense objects according to reason, thoroughly understanding that there are no atoms external to the mind, nor any composite phenomena external to the mind.
All that is seen, heard, sensed, and touched is merely the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) transformed by one’s own consciousness;

this very [aspect] serves as the object-condition (*ālambana*) for consciousness, and it also assists in the arising of consciousness. This is called the first gate of the Mahāyāna contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*).
The treatise is divided into two parts: first, the refutation of external attachments; second, the presentation of the correct principle. First, the external attachments: [Text continues...]
Three. First, the direct refutation of the two positions; second, the refutation of various counter-arguments; third, the conclusion that [the object] is not external form.

The first [section] also has three parts: first, a general statement of the refutation; second, a specific refutation by means of denial; third, the conclusion that it contradicts reason. Now, the first.

Regarding those who maintain that the five consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness, take external forms as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), some hold that atoms (*paramāṇu*) exist as substantial entities capable of producing consciousness;
others hold that it is the composite (*saṃghāta*), because when consciousness arises, it bears the image of that [composite].
Both [positions] are unreasonable. Why is this so?
It is because it is said that the non-Buddhists and the followers of the Lesser Vehicle do not realize that there are no phenomena external to the mind;

therefore, they falsely establish their own doctrines, wishing to claim that the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, do not take the images transformed by themselves as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), but rather [take something else].
Regarding the external five objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*):

some maintain that atoms (*paramāṇu*) external to the mind constitute the objective condition, falsely asserting that these subtle particles possess substantial reality because they can produce consciousness.

Others maintain that the composite objects formed by the aggregation of atoms external to the mind constitute the objective condition, on the grounds that when consciousness arises, it bears their image. This is a general summary.
These are the two kinds of false attachments. The phrase "both are irrational" refutes them by means of reason in general.
The phrase "Why is this so? introduces the following text. II. Refuting the two [theories] individually. A. Refuting the atom (*paramāṇu*). B. Refuting the composite (*saṃghāta*).
In the first [section], there are two parts: 1. Presenting the verse; 2. Explaining its establishment. Now, the first [part].

Regarding atoms (paramāṇu) in relation to the five consciousnesses: even if they were admitted as conditions (ālambana-pratyaya), they would certainly not be objects of cognition (ālambana). This is because their characteristic marks (lakṣaṇa) do not exist within those consciousnesses, just like the eye-faculty (cakṣur-indriya) and so forth.
The formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: The atoms asserted by [the opponent] are the subject (dharmin).

Even if it is granted that they serve as conditions for the five consciousnesses, the thesis (pakṣa) is that they are definitely not objects of cognition. The reason (hetu) is that the characteristic marks of those atoms cannot be apprehended within the five consciousnesses.

The concordant example is like the sense organs, such as the eye-faculty. Indeed, the five faculties can give rise to the five consciousnesses and thus serve as predominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
However, the five consciousnesses do not arise bearing the characteristics of the five faculties; therefore, they are not objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

Furthermore, let us set aside for a moment the fact that outside of consciousness there are no atoms (*paramāṇu*) to be found; even if we were to concede that atoms truly exist and are capable of producing consciousness, they could only function as predominant conditions.

It takes the ear as its superior object (*ālambana*). How could it be maintained that [the ear] is the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*)? △ Second, the explanation and establishment, which has two parts:
first, the explicit clarification of the meaning of the objective condition; second, the explanation of the verse’s response to the objection regarding its deficiency in meaning. Now, the first part.

Regarding the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya): it refers to the consciousness that takes [an object] as its focus. It is called an "object" because the perceiving consciousness arises bearing the aspect of that [object];
and it is called a "condition" because it possesses substantial reality, serving as the basis upon which the perceiving consciousness relies to arise.
This clarifies the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). It must possess both the sense of being "that which is deliberated upon" and "that which is relied upon.
If either of these two senses is lacking, it cannot be established as an objective condition. △ Second, the commentary on the verse addresses the deficiency of its meaning.

Even if the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of form and so forth possessed substantial reality capable of producing the five consciousnesses, they might be said to have the status of an object (*artha*); however, they are not the objective support (*ālambana*).

Just as the eye-faculty and so forth are not the objective support for the visual consciousness and the others because they lack the appearance of those [objects], likewise these atoms lack the status of an objective support for the visual consciousness and the others.
That is to say, regarding those atoms (paramāṇu) of form and so forth which they grasp: for the time being, let us set aside the fact that they fundamentally lack the nature of real dharmas;

even if one were to grant that they possess substantial reality capable of producing the five consciousnesses and thus could potentially serve as objects, they are nonetheless not the *ālambana* (objective referent).
This is because, like the five sense organs such as the eye, they do not arise in the eye-consciousness and so forth bearing their image (*nimitta*). The same applies to these atoms. Regarding...

Since the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth have no objective referent (*ālambana*), how can they be designated as having an "objective-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*)? II. Refuting the Conjunction.
This has two parts: first, the presentation of the verse; second, the explanation. Now, the first.

It is conjoined with the five consciousnesses; even if it were admitted to be an object of cognition, it would not be a causal condition, because its substance does not truly exist, just like a second moon.

The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: that which is asserted to be "conjoined" is a subject of the proposition (*dharmin*); even if it were granted to be an object of the five consciousnesses, [it would still not be a causal condition].

This is the thesis that [the object] is definitely not a causal condition (*pratyaya*). The reason (*hetu*) is stated: "Because those composite objects possess only a conventional appearance while their substance is actually non-existent.
The concordant example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like a second moon; for a second moon is a false perception resulting from pressing the eyes, and its substance is actually non-existent.

However, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is not an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). It is not an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), nor does it serve as a condition for the arising of visual consciousness.
Since it lacks the status of being a condition, how could the status of being an "object of cognition" (*ālambana*) possibly be established? This has been stated merely by way of concession.
△ Second, the explanation and establishment [of the argument].

The aggregation of form and so forth possesses those characteristics within visual consciousness and the like; thus, even if it were made an object of cognition (*ālambana*), it lacks the true meaning of being an object.
This is like a visual disorder where one sees a second moon: that [second moon] has no substantial reality and cannot produce [a cognition]. Such is the case with this aggregation.
Regarding the visual consciousness and the others, there is no sense of an objective referent (*ālambana*).

This is because the composite appearance of external forms and so forth—which they [the opponents] maintain to exist outside the mind—arises in the visual consciousness and other cognitions as if bearing those very characteristics.
Even if it were possible for such an object to serve as a referent, it cannot function as the causal condition for the arising of the consciousness.
The meaning is as follows: For example, due to a visual disorder, one may see a second moon;

yet that second moon has no original substantial reality and cannot produce a direct sensory perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the eye-consciousness, because it is merely an object of the non-valid mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

In the same way, the characteristic of a composite (*saṃghāta*) as it is grasped likewise resembles the second moon; it does not exist as an object for the eye-consciousness and other sensory cognitions.

As for "meaning" (*artha*): since there is no meaning to be apprehended, how could it possibly function as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)? △ Third, the conclusion on the contradiction with reason:
Therefore, regarding these two external things, each lacks one of the two factors required for an object-condition; thus, both are logically untenable.

That is to say, the two things they maintain—the external atoms apart from the mind and the characteristic of their aggregation—each lack one of the necessary factors for the definition of an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*);
therefore, both are unreasonable. This concludes the first section: the direct refutation of the two positions.
△ Second, the refutation of various alternative positions has two parts: first, the refutation of the characteristic of atoms aggregating; second, the refutation of atoms aggregating.
Section on the [False] Aspect. This consists of two parts: first, the statement of the position; second, its refutation. Now, for the first part:
Some maintain that form and so forth each possess many aspects (*ākāra*), among which one portion is the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Therefore, the atoms (*paramāṇu*) mutually support one another, such that each possesses a single aspect of aggregation (*saṃcita*). This aspect is substantially real and is capable of producing a cognition that resembles its own aspect.
Therefore, they serve as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the five consciousnesses.
This means that there is a false attachment to various objects such as form (*rūpa*), which each possess many kinds of combined and differentiated conventional characteristics (*prajñapti-lakṣaṇa*).

Within these, one portion consists of the fundamental atoms (*paramāṇu*). These are the objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Thus, because the various atomic characteristics mutually support one another, they [also]...
Each possesses a characteristic of aggregation (*saṃghāta-lakṣaṇa*). Since this characteristic of aggregation is not separate from the atoms (*paramāṇu*), it is substantially existent (*dravyasat*).
Furthermore, this substantially existent characteristic of aggregation is each capable of producing a consciousness that appears similar to its own form.

Because it thus possesses both meanings—arising while bearing that form and being supported by that [form] to arise—it serves as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the five consciousnesses.
It is a condition (*pratyaya*). △ Second, the refutation:

This is also irrational. Why? Because, like solidity and so forth, even if they were conditions for visual consciousness and the others, they would not be objects (*ālambana*), since you admit that they possess the characteristics of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
The *Pramāṇa* states: "The aggregate aspect upon those grasped atoms is the subject (*dharmin*).

It is the thesis that it is not an object-condition (*ālambana*) for visual consciousness and the other sensory cognitions. The reason (*hetu*) is: because they admit that the aggregate aspect is not separate from the aspect of the atoms.
The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is like solidity, moisture, and so forth; for example, solidity, moisture, and the like do not exist apart from the atoms."

Even if one were to grant that solidity and so forth exist substantially, they might serve as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for visual consciousness and the like, but they certainly cannot be the objective referent (*ālambana*).

This is because visual consciousness and the others do not arise bearing the characteristics of solidity, moisture, and so forth. Now, the same applies to the characteristic of the composite aggregate;
even if one grants it exists substantially, it does not transcend the characteristics of the atoms (*paramāṇu*). How, then, could it function as an objective referent?
Is it not reasonable?

For although characteristics such as solidity may be admitted to exist substantially, they can still serve as conditions (or aids for the arising) for visual consciousness and the other sensory cognitions.
Furthermore, because those characteristics (such as solidity) do not exist within the visual consciousness and so forth,

it follows by logical necessity that the various composite characteristics of the atoms of form and so on must likewise be absent. This is because both [the characteristic of solidity and the characteristic of compositeness] are grasped as being characteristics of the atom itself.
A further explanation of the meaning of the verse may be understood from the text itself. △ Second, the refutation of the state of the aggregation of atoms, in two parts:
first, the presentation of the [opponent’s] position; second, the refutation. Now, the first.
The consciousnesses of the eye and so forth apprehend the aggregated characteristics of atoms; yet there is another [consciousness] that arises.

Since the aggregated characteristic upon the atom has already been refuted above, even if there were an object that serves as a basis for cognition, it would not be a true objective support (*ālambana*).

Now, this further evolves into another position: namely, that upon the atoms (*paramāṇu*), various collective characteristics (*saṃcita-lakṣaṇa*) arise, and furthermore, distinct formal characteristics (*ākāra-lakṣaṇa*) emerge, which can serve as the objects (*ālambana*) of visual and other consciousnesses.

Therefore, it is said that visual and other consciousnesses are able to take as their objects these distinct [formal] characteristics that arise from the collective characteristics of the atoms. However, since these collective characteristics...
If they were not distinct from atoms, and atoms themselves were not distinct, then the characteristics of cognition would likewise have to be non-distinct.
Since the characteristics of cognition are indeed distinct, atoms must also be distinct. Now, it is untenable to claim that the characteristics of cognition are non-distinct;
yet it is also untenable to claim that atoms are distinct. Is this not a case where what you maintain is merely an increase in error? Therefore, the following [text] addresses these two points.
Refutation. △ Second, the refutation and censure, which has two parts. First, the refutation based on the fact that cognitions should have no distinction.
Second, the refutation based on the distinction of atoms. Now, the first:

Regarding the characteristics of the cognitions of jars, bowls, and so forth, according to their [the opponents'] tenets, there should be no distinction between them. It is not because of a difference in shape that they are distinct, for a difference in shape is not real.
This refers to the cognitive aspect that takes jars, bowls, and so forth as its objects. If one adheres to that [position], there should be no further distinction.
Why? Because both the jar and the bowl are equally the aspect of an aggregation (*saṃcita*) of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Thus, regarding this aspect of aggregation, how could there be room for a distinct cognition of "jar" versus "bowl"? It cannot be said that [the difference lies] in the jar, the bowl, etc.,...

The distinctions in shape entail distinctions in cognition, because these distinctions in shape exist only within conventional (prajñapti) phenomena and not within real atoms (paramāṇu), as atoms themselves possess no differentiation.
If atoms were without distinction, then cognition likewise would have to be without distinction.
Regarding objects such as jars and bowls, whether large or small, they are identical in terms of the number of atoms that constitute them;

therefore, the cognitions apprehending them should likewise be without distinction. If it is argued that the cognitions differ because the shapes and physical characteristics of those objects differ, this is also logically untenable.
The distinct shapes of the neck and so forth exist only upon provisional phenomena such as vases; they do not belong to the atoms themselves.

This is a further explanation of the meaning of the verse. That is to say, if one maintains that consciousness arises by taking atoms in their aggregated state as its object, then for objects such as vases or bowls where the dimensions are equal, the number of atoms that constitute them [would have to differ].
Because they are determined to be identical, the cognitive aspects that take those two objects as their conditions should likewise have no difference between them.
For instance, consider a single jar weighing about one jin, which is composed of a collection of a certain number of atoms.
Furthermore, there is another bowl that likewise weighs about one *jin*. It too is composed of a collection of a certain number of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Since the number of atoms that constitute these two objects is identical, the mental states that take these two objects as their objects should likewise have no difference in their aspects (*ākāra*).
If it is argued that the aspects of the mental states differ because the shapes and substances of the objects are distinct...

As for the claim that there is distinction [between atoms], this is also unreasonable. Because various distinct shapes, such as those of the neck and belly, exist only upon conventional phenomena like jars and bowls, one cannot say that atoms themselves possess differentiation.

Since there is no difference in the number or aggregation of atoms, the perceived characteristics (*buddhi-lakṣaṇa*) should likewise be without distinction. Yet, since perceived characteristics do indeed possess distinctions, it cannot be [the case that they arise from atoms].
It is clear that the aggregation of atoms constitutes the objective referent (ālambana). II. Refutation by way of the differentiation of atoms:
One should not maintain that atoms themselves possess differentiated shapes. Why is this?

Having already clarified that since atoms aggregate without distinction, cognition should likewise be without distinction, [the author] anticipates the opponent’s counter-argument that atoms themselves possess distinctions, and thus causes the characteristics of cognition to appear distinct; he then subjects this to scrutiny and refutes it.

Because they are equal in being infinitesimal particles (*paramāṇu*), the distinction of shape exists only conventionally (*prajñapti*). When those [objects] are analyzed down to the ultimate particle, the cognition of them is necessarily abandoned;

therefore, jars, bowls, and the like cannot constitute ultimate particles with distinct shapes and dimensions. Since they abandon the characteristic of minute sphericity, one knows that the distinction of shape exists only conventionally and is not real.

Furthermore, when objects of distinct shape are analyzed down to the ultimate particle, the cognition of them is necessarily abandoned, whereas this is not the case for substances such as blue and so forth.

When analyzed down to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), that cognition can be abandoned. Therefore, these distinct shapes exist only conventionally (*saṃvṛti-sat*), and do not exist as real entities (*dravya*) in the same way that blue and other such qualities do.
First the verse is presented, and then it is explained. The explanation states: "It cannot be said that the [atoms] which constitute pots, bowls, and so forth, are themselves the ultimate..."
Even the subtle possesses distinctions of form and magnitude, yet it ultimately abandons its characteristics of subtlety and roundness.
Therefore, one should know that various distinct shapes such as the neck and belly exist only in conventional phenomena (prajñapti-dharma), not in ultimate phenomena (paramārtha-dharma).

Herein, for the time being, the atom (paramāṇu) is provisionally designated as an ultimate phenomenon. Furthermore, regarding distinct objects of shape, even if they are analyzed down to the atom, those distinct shapes [do not persist].

The cognition of these [parts] is necessarily abandoned. For example, if a single jar and a single bowl are simultaneously smashed to pieces, the cognition of "jar" or "bowl" will certainly not arise, nor can one possibly distinguish which atoms belong to the jar.

Who is it that perceives the atom of a jar? Even if objects such as blue or yellow are analyzed down to their ultimate atoms, one still perceives blue as blue and yellow as yellow; it cannot be said that the perception of them is also abandoned.

Therefore, distinctions of shape exist only conventionally (saṃvṛti), unlike blue and other qualities which exist both as real entities and conventionally. These conventional existents are precisely the four conventional truths.

The provisional names within this [category] are not subsumed under the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and cannot serve as conditions to produce visual consciousness and the other sense-consciousnesses;

they are merely objects of the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). As for substantial entities (*dravya*), these correspond to the "truth of differentiation according to phenomena" (*vastu-bheda-satya*) among the four conventional truths, and also to the "truth of the manifestation of essence and function" (*svabhāva-kārya-prakāśana-satya*) among the four ultimate truths. Now, regarding colors such as blue and yellow... [the text continues].

This objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) transformed by the visual consciousness itself is called the "objective realm" (*xingjing*). Therefore, it is said that [the blue color] "also exists as a real entity.

However, the two characters "also exists" (*yì zài*) are intended to clarify that while the conventional designation (*nāmavāda*) such as "blue" is not a real entity, the essential nature and characteristics (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*) of the blue color are.
This is merely a real entity that is a transformation of consciousness. This concludes the second section: Refuting Various Erroneous Theories. △ Third, concluding that it is not external matter:
Therefore, the nature of the objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya) for the five consciousnesses is not external matter and so forth; this principle is thoroughly established.
Since atoms cannot serve as objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*), nor can their aggregation serve as an objective condition,
and since neither the characteristic of the collection of atoms nor the state of the collection of atoms can serve as an objective condition,
how could those external forms and so forth, which you maintain to exist apart from the mind, possibly exist?

It can indeed function as the substantial basis for the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "If one were to grant the existence of atoms (*paramāṇu*), this fault would still ensue;
how much more so when there are no real atoms external to consciousness? This is what that means. The above concludes the true refutation.
Therefore, it is concluded: "The principle is fully established. II. Presenting the Correct Doctrine. This has two parts: first, the actual establishment.
First, it is established that internal objects of perception exist as conditions; second, it is simultaneously established that the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) is not non-existent;
third, the conclusion concerns only internal objects. Regarding the first two [points], there are two parts: first, the formal establishment; second, the resolution of doubts. Now, for the first:
Could it be that their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) does not exist at all? It is not the case that it does not exist at all.
If so, how is it? This is posed as a question and answer to raise the point for examination. The question asks:

If, as has been refuted above, neither individual atoms nor their aggregation can serve as an object-condition, then could it be that the object-condition for those five consciousnesses does not exist at all?
"Is there [such a thing]? He replied, "It is not that it does not exist at all. Again, he asked:
"If that is so, since external form is not the substance of the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya), then how, ultimately, can that which you call the 'object-condition' exist?"
"Internal form appears as if external; it serves as the objective condition for consciousness. We maintain that its aspect resides within consciousness, because it can give rise to consciousness.
This first verse provides the response. "Internal form" refers to the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of form transformed by consciousness.

"Appearing as if external" means that it does not originally exist outside the mind; rather, it is because sentient beings fail to realize that the essence of the mind has never had anything external to it from the outset.
One falsely identifies the four great elements as the characteristic of one's own body, and falsely identifies the mind as being within the physical body;

therefore, regarding the forms manifested by one's own consciousness, they appear as if they were external. Thus, these internal forms that appear as if external serve as the objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the visual and other consciousnesses.
It is admitted that while their appearance resides within consciousness, they possess the status of being an object of cognition. And...
It is capable of producing consciousness because it possesses the characteristic of being an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

Although external objects do not exist, internal forms that appear similar to external objects serve as the object-condition, because it is admitted that visual and other consciousnesses bear their images and arise from them;
thus, they possess both of these two characteristics.

This is a further explanation of the meaning of the verse. Although external objects do not exist—meaning that from the beginning there has been no phenomenon outside of the mind—they appear as if they were external objects;

this means that they are conventionally designated as "external" in accordance with common perception. "Bearing their aspect" (sākāra) signifies that it possesses the quality of being an object of cognition (*ālambana*).

"Arising from them" signifies that it further possesses the quality of being a condition (*pratyaya*). Since these two meanings are complete and lacking nothing, it is truly a valid proof (*sādhana*).
[End of section]. △ Second, resolving doubts, which has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer and explanation. Now, the first:
Since these internal objective aspects do not exist apart from consciousness, how can they arise simultaneously and yet function as conditions for that consciousness?
Since they arise simultaneously, there is no sequence of before and after; how, then, can they act as conditions for the arising of consciousness? Thus the question is raised.
△ Second, the answer and explanation:
Because they necessarily follow one another, they also act as conditions at the same time; or, the preceding acts as a condition for the succeeding by inducing its functional capacity.
Because the objective aspect (*viṣaya-nimitta*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are necessarily concomitant, even though they arise simultaneously, the former still acts as a condition for the latter.

Proponents of the theory of causal efficacy (*satkāryavāda*) maintain that if one thing follows the presence or absence of another, then even though they arise at the same time, they may nonetheless possess the relationship of cause and effect.

Alternatively, the aspect of a preceding consciousness serves as the condition for a subsequent consciousness, inducing the arising of a capacity within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) that manifests as its own result;
this does not contradict reason.
Thus, first the verse is presented, and subsequently it is explained and established. The objective aspect of the internal mind and the consciousness that takes it as its object are determinate.
Because they follow one another, even though they arise simultaneously, they can still serve as conditions for consciousness. As the masters of the *Hetuvidyā* (Logic) state:

"If this phenomenon and that phenomenon exist together when it exists, and do not exist when it does not exist—if their existence and non-existence follow one another—then even though they are produced at the same time, because 'this exists' [implies] 'that exists,' this is precisely the cause."
"Characteristics. This refers to the fact that they serve as the characteristics of the fruit. This explains the meaning of the first two lines of the verse.
Furthermore, the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of a preceding consciousness can serve as the generative condition (*janaka-pratyaya*) for a subsequent consciousness.

When the *nimitta-bhāga* of the five active consciousnesses perfumes the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), it is able to induce the arising of a capacity within that fundamental consciousness to produce a semblance of its own fruit. It also...
"Because it does not contradict correct reasoning. This explains the meaning of the latter two lines of the verse.
"Producing a capacity that resembles its own fruit" refers to the five pure material sense organs (*pañca-rūpa-prasāda*), which are able to produce the five active consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).

Therefore, the five consciousnesses produced are called "resembling the fruit of the eye," and the five organs capable of producing them are termed "capacities. First, this correctly establishes the internal [bases].

The section on the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) as existence is concluded. △ Second, establishing the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) concurrently by showing that it is not non-existent.
Part one: posing the question and citing the verse. Part two: explaining and establishing it through the treatise. Now, the first part.
If the five consciousnesses arise taking only internal form as their object, how can it also be said that the eye and so forth serve as conditions?
This question is posed to address the meaning of the Sūtra’s teaching that visual consciousness and the rest arise with the eye and form as conditions.

The functional capacity for form within consciousness is appropriately termed the "five faculties. This capacity and its objective counterpart, form, have served as mutual causes since beginningless time.
This was first answered briefly in verse. That is to say, the functional capacity for form within the eighth consciousness is designated as the five faculties;
this accords with correct principle. Furthermore, this very capacity and those objective forms of the *nimitta-bhāga* (perceived aspect) have existed as such since beginningless time.
They constantly act as causes for one another, mutually perfuming and giving rise [to each other]. △ Second, the explanation and establishment by means of the treatise, which has two parts:
first, the explanation of the preceding two lines; second, the explanation of the subsequent two lines. Now, the first part.
Because consciousness can arise, one infers the existence of the faculties (indriya). These are merely functional capacities (śakti) and are not produced by external matter.

Therefore, it is not contrary to reason to designate the five types of functional capacities upon the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) as the "eye-faculty" and so forth. This is because there is no logical distinction between a functional capacity giving rise to consciousness and what is conventionally called a faculty.

Although it cannot be said whether [the sense-faculties] exist in consciousness or elsewhere, because external dharmas do not exist in principle, one must certainly admit that they exist in consciousness and not elsewhere.

The five pure material faculties (pañca-rūpa-prasāda) are not obtained through direct perception (pratyakṣa), for they are inferred (anumāna) by virtue of their capacity to give rise to consciousness.
To know that there are faculties (*indriya*) means that these are merely functional capacities upon the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the eighth consciousness;

they do not exist as eight distinct entities produced externally to the mind. Therefore, it is not contrary to reason to designate the five kinds of pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*)—which are functional capacities within the fundamental consciousness—as the five faculties, such as the eye-faculty and so forth.
It is precisely these capacities that can give rise to the five consciousnesses; there is no principle for their existence outside of the mind.

Because it is a distinct dharma. However, since the five sense faculties are known through inference and are not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it cannot be said whether they reside in consciousness or elsewhere.
Yet, because external dharmas apart from the mind do not exist in principle, one must certainly admit this functional capacity.
It is determined that this resides in consciousness and not elsewhere. △ Second, the explanation of the latter two phrases has two parts: first, the direct explanation;
second, the discussion of identity and difference. Now, for the first:
this faculty’s capacity and the preceding objective form have served as reciprocal causes from the beginningless past. That is to say, this capacity...

Upon reaching the stage of maturation, it gives rise to the five internal objective forms upon the manifest consciousness; these internal objective forms, in turn, are able to induce the functional capacities of the five sense organs upon the retributive consciousness.
This refers to the functional capacities of the five sense organs (*pañcendriya*) upon this eighth consciousness.

These function as causes for one another, in turn, with the objective forms (*rūpa*) that are the perceived objects (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the previously mentioned five consciousnesses, from beginningless time. How is this known?

It is because when all the functional capacities within this fundamental consciousness reach their state of maturation, they are able to produce the five [sensory] manifestations upon the active five consciousnesses.

The objective forms within the internal image-aspects (*antar-vibhāga*) of these [five consciousnesses]—that is, the objective forms within the internal image-aspects of these five consciousnesses—further perfume the root consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), giving rise to the functional capacities of the five sense organs upon the maturation-consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*).
Therefore, it is said that from time immemorial they act as mutual causes for one another.
△ Second, the differentiation of identity and difference.

Regarding the two types of form—sense faculties and objects—one may explain them as being either identical to or different from consciousness, or neither identical nor different, according to one's preference.

The pure matter of the five sense faculties and the objective matter of the primary substance are the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the eighth consciousness. The objective matter that serves as the *ālambana-pratyaya* (cognitive object-condition) for the first five consciousnesses is the *nimitta-bhāga* of those five consciousnesses.
In all cases, the *nimitta-bhāga* and *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect) are not separate from the essence of self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*).
Therefore, it may be said that they are one; yet since the object of cognition (*ālambana*) is not the cognizing subject (*ālambaka*), it may also be said that they are different.

Furthermore, because of the distinction between the image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), they are not one; yet because they are not separate from self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), they are not different. Moreover, as cause and effect, essence and function, they are neither identical nor distinct.
Thus, having realized that all phenomena (*dharma*) fundamentally lack an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), one may speak of them according to one's inclination. (2) Combined.
The establishment of the predominating condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) based on its non-absence is concluded. △ Third, the conclusion that objects are exclusively internal:
Thus, it is well-established by reason that these various consciousnesses have only the aspects of internal objects as their object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).

"Various consciousnesses" refers, for the time being, to the first five consciousnesses. "Internal objective aspects" refers to the *nimitta-bhāga* (perceived aspect) manifested by each respective consciousness itself.
Since the five consciousnesses do not take external objects as their conditions, [this applies] from the sixth consciousness up to the seventh and eighth consciousnesses.
It is thus clearly established that there are no objects of cognition external to the mind; therefore, it is said that the principle is well-established.
This is what is meant by a "true proof" (*sādhana*).
*A Direct Commentary on the Treatise on Examining the Conditions of Objects of Cognition* (End).
